title: Hammadid Dynasty
capsule: The Hammadid dynasty was a Berber Ṣinhāja ruling house that governed a kingdom centered on the high plateau of northeastern Algeria from 1014 to 1152, founded by Ḥammād ibn Buluggīn, a nephew of the Fatimid client Zīrī ibn Manād. At its height the dynasty controlled territory from the Saharan margins to the coast, ruling from the Qala'a of the Banu Hammad — a fortified palatial city in the Hodna region that UNESCO now recognizes as a World Heritage Site. The Hammadids came under severe pressure from the Hilalian Arab tribal influx (from c. 1052), which disrupted agriculture and shifted demographic patterns across the Maghreb; the dynasty was ultimately extinguished when the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mumin besieged and captured Béjaïa (Bougie), the last Hammadid capital, in 1152.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core domain around the Qal'a and Béjaïa is well established; outer limits toward the Sahara and the Tlemcen corridor varied with Zayyanid and Almoravid competition and are imprecisely mapped.
